Holding dominant harmony for a long stretch, so that a return or arrival is delayed and expected.
Stripping a theme down, motif by motif, until only a fragment or a single chord is left, often before a return.
A small motif carried across a join, so the new section feels derived from the old even when key, texture and tempo change.
A sign, an arc over a dot, that holds a note or rest beyond its written length; the performer decides how long.
Silence for the whole ensemble at once: a deliberate break that stops the music before it restarts.
The pause in a sonata exposition that separates the first group from the second theme, usually after a half cadence on the dominant.
A long, gradual increase in force that carries the music towards a climax, by adding instruments, notes, register or speed.
A gradual fall in loudness; at a join it can clear space for the next section or let a climax dissolve.
A shift in how the parts are layered: solo to ensemble, melody and accompaniment to counterpoint, chords to running notes.
A change in who plays the music — a melody handed to other instruments, a section dropped or added — that marks or shapes the join.
A move into a much higher or lower pitch range, which changes the weight and colour of the music at a join.
A shift of speed marked in the score, such as Largo to Moderato, that signals a new section.
A change of time signature or beat grouping, which alters how the pulse is felt.
A short passage written to connect two sections: no new theme, only the harmony and motion that lead from one to the other.
A passage for the soloist alone in a concerto or aria, displaying technique over a pause on the dominant; originally improvised.
Italian “attack”: an instruction to go straight on to the next movement without a pause.
